newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Yields on Kazakh T-bills to fall steadily - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Yields on Kazakh T-bills to fall steadily - dealers.

text.p: Yields on Treasury bills in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan are likely to fall steadily both in the short and long term, dealers said on Friday.
"I expect that T-bill (GKO) yields will go down at auctions next week," Denis Fedosenko, dealer at Kazkommertsbank said.

Six-month GKOs will be auctioned on Monday and three-month paper on Tuesday. Six-month T-bills yielded 30.81 percent at the previous auction on January 20, while three-month paper yielded 25.40 percent on January 29.
"The demand for T-bills is big, the more so now as banks have money after the redemption of three-month T-bills by the Finance Ministry on January 30," he said.
Other dealers said they expected yields to continue falling in coming months.

"My general view is that yields on GKOs are likely to fall steadily due to lowering inflation, the relatively stable tenge currency and the participation of foreign investors," said Serik Zhukenov of ABN-AMRO Bank Kazakhstan, a unit of Dutch-owned bank ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
Foreign investors are entitled to buy only 20-30 percent of each GKO issue but Zhukenov said "they have already started competing seriously with local banks".
Zhukenov predicted the Kazakh tenge would be "more or less stable" in 1997. The government aims to cut inflation this year to 21 percent from 28.7 percent in 1996.
"But even if the tenge loses some 10 or 12 percent, foreigners will not be scared off and will remain active," Zhukenov said.
Foreign buyers, who invested 800 million tenge last year in Kazakh GKOs, are watching the Kazakh debt market with growing interest.
"Kazakh debt is definitely on the radar for foreign investors after the Eurobond issue," a Western economist told Reuters.

Substantial demand for Kazakhstan's debut Eurobond last December prompted the government to double its originally planned $100 million issue. Investors, principally funds in the United States and Europe, snapped up the enlarged issue.
